newsitem.title: UK: Currency moves dominate Euro vegetable oil market.
newsitem.headline: Currency moves dominate Euro vegetable oil market.

text.p: Currency factors dominated the European vegetable oil market at the opening on Friday, traders said.
The Malaysian ringgit came under further pressure, hitting its lowest level, 2.8250, against the U.S. dollar since it was officially floated in 1973.
The newly floated Indonesia rupiah also ran into a storm of selling, hitting a new low of 2,890 against the dollar.

The combined impact of these losses and latest data from the Malaysian Palm oil Registration and Licensing Authority (PORLA) pushed palm oil prices higher in Asia, although the full impact of this is unlikely to hit the European market until Monday because of holidays in many countries.
PORLA pegged Malaysian palm oil output at 833,159 tonnes during July against 791,426 in June, a rise of 5.27 percent.
Exports were 715,906 tonnes against 622,210 tonnes in June, while stocks fell from 789,806 tonnes at end-June to 769,275 tonnes at end-July, a fall of 2.6 percent.
The Malaysian Oil Palm Growers' Council released dated before PORLA and put output at 828,000 tonnes in July, 5.1 percent from June.
In its estimate for the first 15 days of August cargo surveyor SGS put local palm oil exports at 312,757 tonnes against 307,536 during the same period in June.
"To say today's figures have been friendly is an understatement, but a lot of the increase we have seen this morning are due to currency," said one trader.
At the opening, crude palm oil cif Europe was $2.50 up after Oct/Dec traded at $512.50 a tonne, while olein fetched $525 and $527.50 a tonne fob Malaysian ports for Sept and $522.50 for Oct/Dec.
Lauric oils took their lead from palm oil, with opening sellers $2.50 to $5 higher.
Higher Chicago soyoil futures underpinned soft oils, with sellers one to two guilders up, but buyers were showing little interest.
"The Chicago market has been relegated to side-show status until we see the harvest," said one trader.
